evidence_spans: This paper investigated the effects of different crystal orientations, temperatures, and strain rates on the mechanical properties and plastic deformation mechanisms of an equiatomic FeNiCrMn HEA using molecular dynamics simulations.
The results revealed that the FeNiCrMn HEA exhibited significant anisotropy under loading along different orientations, with the maximum yield stress observed along the <11-1> direction.
During the elastic stage, all crystals maintained a single FCC structure.
As strain increased, yielding occurred, accompanied by a sudden drop in stress, which was attributed to the generation of dislocations.
The mechanical properties of the FeNiCrMn HEA were highly sensitive to temperature variations.
Elevated temperatures intensify atomic thermal vibrations, making it easier for atoms to deviate from their equilibrium positions and facilitating dislocation nucleation and movement.
Consequently, the yield strength and yield strain decreased with increasing temperature.
In contrast, the yield strength of the FeNiCrMn HEA was relatively insensitive to strain rate variations.
During tensile loading, higher strain rates led to higher dislocation densities.
When the stress stabilized, the flow stress increased with the strain rate.

parameters.potential: EAM (Daw et al. and Daramola et al.)

process_steps.resulting_state: Deformed structures with dislocations and stacking faults

structure_observations.qualitative_value: FCC to HCP (via stacking faults), no BCC observed
Stacking faults (ISF/ESF), not true phase transformation

test_conditions.thermal_history: Heated to 1000 K, held, cooled to 300 K, held
test_conditions.simulation_conditions: Periodic boundaries, 1 fs time step, Nose-Hoover thermostat

measurements.method: Elastic stage slope of stress-strain curve

comparison.baseline_description: Reference equiatomic FeNiCrMn model at 300 K, 10^9 s^-1

mechanisms.assertion: Dislocation nucleation initiates at vacancy clusters formed by disordered atoms.
supported_by: Observation of vacancies preceding dislocation loops in DXA analysis
Spatial correlation of disordered atoms and dislocation nucleation sites
mechanisms.discriminating_measurement: Vacancy concentration vs. strain at nucleation onset

mechanisms.assertion: Plastic deformation is mediated by Shockley partial dislocations creating stacking faults (ISF/ESF).
supported_by: CNA analysis showing HCP-like regions corresponding to 1/6<112> dislocations
mechanisms.discriminating_measurement: Absence of twin boundaries in CNA/DXA

mechanisms.assertion: Yield strength decreases with temperature due to reduced critical resolved shear stress and enhanced thermal vibration.
supported_by: Decreasing yield strength in stress-strain curves at 300K vs 600K
Increased dislocation mobility observed in DXA

limitations.description: Simulations conducted at nanoscale with high strain rates (10^8-10^10 s^-1) compared to experiments.
limitations.impact: May not fully capture macroscopic strain rate sensitivity or long-range dislocation interactions.

limitations.description: Single crystal model used; grain boundary effects not included.
limitations.impact: Results may differ from polycrystalline bulk behavior.

limitations.description: Strain rate range limited; sensitivity might exist outside tested range.
limitations.impact: Conclusions on strain rate insensitivity apply only to the simulated range.

evidence_spans: The primary dislocations observed were Shockley partial dislocations and stair-rod immobile dislocations.
No BCC atoms were observed in any of the three orientations, indicating that no FCC-to-BCC phase transformation occurred during tensile deformation.
The yield strength of the alloy was relatively insensitive to strain rate within the simulated range.

structure_observations.qualitative_value: FCC to HCP phase transformation, stacking fault, grain refinement, twinning

mechanisms.assertion: FCC to HCP phase transformation, stacking fault, grain refinement, and twinning occur during plastic deformation of HEAs.

evidence_spans: Qi et al. [ [14] ] analyzed the plastic deformation of single-crystal and polycrystalline CoCrFeMnNi HEAs under tension and compression using MD simulations. The simulation results indicated that during the plastic deformation of the HEA material, phenomena such as FCC to HCP phase transformation, stacking fault, grain refinement, and twinning occurred.

structure_observations.qualitative_value: Increased temperature/Cu reduces properties; increased strain rate enhances properties

mechanisms.assertion: Increasing temperature and Cu content reduces mechanical properties, while increasing strain rate enhances them; cracks accelerate plastic deformation.

evidence_spans: Wang et al. [ [15] ] simulated the tensile process of crack-free and cracked FeNiCrCoCu HEAs under different temperatures, strain rates, and Cu content. The results showed that increasing temperature and Cu content reduced the mechanical properties of the HEA, while increasing strain rate enhanced the mechanical properties of the HEA. The presence of cracks accelerated the plastic deformation of the HEA.
